To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ionization radiation from O stars is a key process for the evolution of molecular clouds.
the ionization of massive stars drives turbulence in their environment and triggers star formation.
UV radiation of massive O-stars can drive the turbulent ISM and trigger star formation by compressing the gas and forming pillars.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how ionizing radiation from hot massive stars influences the formation of stars in molecular clouds.
the question how ionizing radiation of hot stars influences the evolution of the surrounding interstellar medium.
the question how stars form from cold molecular clouds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the UV radiation from O stars can be used to explain the formation and evolution of star-forming regions in a self-consistent manner.
UV radiation from hot stars is a major driver for the formation of star-forming structures in the ISM.
ionizing radiation from massive O stars can trigger the formation of low- to intermediate-mass stars by driving and sustaining turbulence in the surrounding ISM.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
UV radiation of massive stars is a very efficient mechanism to trigger and sustain star formation in the Galactic ISM.
UV radiation from hot stars is a powerful mechanism to drive turbulence and to induce gravitational collapse in star-forming clouds.
ionizing radiation of hot stars is able to sustain and drive turbulence and thus to trigger star formation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ISM is a highly dynamic and complex system.
UV radiation of massive stars plays a crucial role in the evolution of star-forming regions and in the triggering of star formation.
the ionizing radiation of hot stars is not just a trigger for star formation but also a driver for turbulence.
